You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.
If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback.

# - <LM_INPUT>: The input to the language model.
# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.
payload.instruction: Make her close her jacket fully
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: Is the woman's jacket visibly closed more than in the input image, with its front panels brought together at least in part?
node.criteria: Pass if the image shows the jacket's front panels brought together along some portion of the closure compared with the input. Fail if the jacket is visibly unchanged or more open. Unknown if the closure cannot be assessed from the image or comparison evidence is insufficient.
node.binding: Assess only the woman's jacket identified in the input image; judge visible change to its front closure, not unrelated edits.

node_traces.evidence: The jacket’s front is visibly more open in the edited image, with a panel hanging away from her body, rather than brought together compared with the source.

fulfillment: The node’s target and completion criterion are clear, but its evidence chain appears to misread the images: the source already shows the jacket front together, while the edited image shows it hanging open. Thus the requested change is not evidenced, and the reference label “yes” should not override that visual evidence. Improve the upstream checks’ source-versus-edit comparison and ensure the fulfillment node faithfully uses their statuses; do not change the criterion or force a positive label. Both checks were valid, queried, and high-confidence with no transport or schema failure, so investigate visual interpretation/binding rather than execution reliability. Keep the binding anchored to the same jacket and distinguish closure from pose or garment movement; retain partial/unknown handling when evidence genuinely warrants it.
s2: The endpoint criterion is clear, but the node’s evidence appears to confuse the jacket’s drape and the woman’s changed pose with an open closure. The edited image shows her turned sideways with the jacket swinging outward; that alone does not establish that an opening remains along the closure. Refine the binding to inspect the closure itself in the edited frame, distinguishing a visible gap between the front panels from fabric displaced by motion or viewpoint. Use unknown when the closure cannot be reliably seen, and preserve partial progress if some closure is visible but incomplete. Keep the full-closure requirement unchanged; the reference label is not atomic ground truth. Both checks ran validly at high confidence, so this is a visual interpretation issue, not a transport or schema failure.
